title: Vasili Arkhipov Refuses to Launch
text:
In October 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, four Soviet diesel submarines were sent toward Cuba. Unknown to the Americans, each carried a torpedo with a nuclear warhead.

On October 27 American destroyers found the submarine B-59 and began dropping small practice depth charges to force it to surface. The submarine had been out of contact with Moscow for days. It was running out of battery power, the temperature inside was extreme, and the air was foul. According to the account of a communications officer aboard, Vadim Orlov, the captain, Valentin Savitsky, concluded that war might already have started. He ordered the nuclear torpedo prepared.

Vasili Arkhipov, the chief of staff of the submarine brigade, was aboard B-59 and equal in rank to the captain. By the accounts of crew members, he argued against firing and calmed Savitsky down. Instead of attacking, B-59 surfaced among the American ships. It turned away and headed back to the Soviet Union.

The episode remained little known until Soviet participants spoke about it at a conference in Havana in 2002. Arkhipov's refusal is now widely seen as one of the moments when the world came closest to nuclear war.
lesson: Under pressure, one person who stays calm and refuses to act on fear can prevent a disaster. Your voice matters most when others are losing theirs.
people: Vasili Arkhipov, Valentin Savitsky, Vadim Orlov
source: Testimony of B-59 crew members, including Vadim Orlov; National Security Archive, The Underwater Cuban Missile Crisis (2012)
caveat: Crew accounts differ on how close the launch came and on whether Arkhipov's formal consent was required.
